title: Giovanni Tozzi Nil Assessment (Aug 2012 TCC) Decision
subject: No Appeal Lies From an Assessment Showing No Tax Payable
summary: Giovanni Tozzi v. The Queen (2010 TCC 545), a Tax Court of Canada nil assessment decision catalogued in 2012 SR&ED jurisprudence, confirms that taxpayers cannot appeal an assessment showing no tax payable, even when the CRA denies a tax credit. For SR&ED claimants in loss years, securing a loss determination or deemed-payment determination is essential to preserve appeal rights.
metaDescription: Learn about the August 2012 Tax Court of Canada decision for Giovanni Tozzi regarding a nil assessment in Canadian tax law.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

In the jurisprudence governing Canadian tax incentives and Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) litigation, few procedural doctrines present as formidable a barrier to taxpayers as the "nil assessment" rule. The decision of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) in Giovanni Tozzi v. Her Majesty The Queen (Docket: 2010-1808(IT)I; Citation: 2010 TCC 545)—heard in Montreal, Quebec, on August 18, 2010, decided by Order of Chief Justice Gerald J. Rip on October 26, 2010, and prominently catalogued in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence repositories in August 2012 under the nil assessment classification—crystallizes the strict jurisdictional boundaries of the Tax Court of Canada when the Minister of National Revenue (the Minister), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), denies a statutory tax credit in a taxation year where no Part I tax is payable.

While the immediate factual catalyst in Tozzi involved an individual taxpayer contesting the CRA's denial of a Disability Tax Credit (DTC) and consequential eligibility for a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) under section 146.4 of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the Act), the nil assessment principle it applies—drawn from earlier case law that the Chief Justice described as being to the effect that there is no appeal from a nil assessment—is frequently invoked in Canadian SR&ED practice, although, as a decision rendered under the Informal Procedure, Tozzi is not itself to be treated as a binding precedent (Tax Court of Canada Act, s. 18.28). Whenever a corporate or individual claimant incurs SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the Act and claims Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), the disallowance of those claims by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR) during a loss year or non-taxable year frequently results in a notification that no tax is payable—a nil assessment. Under the legal framework reaffirmed in Tozzi, a taxpayer cannot appeal a nil assessment to the Tax Court of Canada to obtain a de novo adjudication of their underlying technical or statutory eligibility unless specific statutory exceptions are triggered.

body.text: The Taxpayer's Claim and the Tax Authority's Challenge

In February 2009, the appellant, Giovanni Tozzi, submitted a completed Disability Tax Credit Certificate for the 2008 taxation year, certified by a medical practitioner, to the CRA. The CRA denied him the disability tax credit. The Minister's assessment of the appellant for the 2008 taxation year was a nil assessment—an assessment that no tax is payable—and the appellant did not disagree with the nil assessment as such (the reasons for order do not state why no tax was payable). Although the tax credit would not have altered his immediate tax liability for 2008, the CRA's refusal to recognize the credit disqualified the appellant from attaining status as a "DTC-eligible individual" under subsection 146.4(1) of the Act, which, he said, left him unable to contest the CRA's refusal and therefore unable to be a beneficiary of a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) described in section 146.4 of the Act (and thus of the associated federal grants and bonds), since the Act prohibits contributions to an RDSP if the beneficiary is not a DTC-eligible individual in respect of the taxation year.

Seeking an independent adjudication of his eligibility, the appellant filed a Notice of Appeal with the Tax Court of Canada under the Informal Procedure. Rather than defending the substantive medical or technical merits of the CRA's denial, the Respondent (the Crown) brought a preliminary motion to dismiss the appeal in its entirety on the sole jurisdictional ground that an appeal cannot lie from a nil assessment. The appellant's representative, Vincent Biello, argued that when the Minister denies the disability tax credit and there is a nil assessment for the relevant taxation year, the taxpayer is prohibited from challenging the Minister's denial and is prejudiced in not being permitted to contest it, and further argued that the inability to appeal from a nil assessment ought not to apply to appeals from assessments for 2008 and later where the issue relates to RDSP eligibility, because a taxpayer must have a right to contest the Minister's decisions even when the tax assessment is nil.
The Governing Statutory Framework and Final Holding

Chief Justice Rip emphasized the limited jurisdiction of the Tax Court in hearing matters under the Income Tax Act, noting that the Tax Court of Canada is a superior court to which a taxpayer dissatisfied with an assessment of income tax may appeal that assessment. Pursuant to section 12 of the Tax Court of Canada Act and subsection 169(1) of the Act, a taxpayer's right of appeal to the Tax Court is strictly confined to contesting an "assessment" of tax, interest, or penalties. Furthermore, subsection 171(1) of the Act exhaustively circumscribes how the Tax Court may dispose of an appeal: the Court may only (a) dismiss it, or (b) allow it and (i) vacate the assessment, (ii) vary the assessment, or (iii) refer the assessment back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment.

Relying on case law to the effect that there is no appeal from a nil assessment—a principle traceable to the Supreme Court of Canada's ruling in Okalta Oils Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue (which is not itself cited in the Tozzi reasons) and reflected in the decisions cited in footnote 1 of the reasons, namely the Exchequer Court's decision in Newfoundland Minerals Ltd. v. M.N.R. (69 DTC 5432) and the Federal Court of Appeal's decisions in The Queen v. Gary Bowl Ltd. (74 DTC 6401), Bowater Mersey Paper Co. Ltd. v. The Queen (87 DTC 5382), and The Queen v. Interior Savings Credit Union (2007 FCA 151 / 2007 DTC 5342)—Chief Justice Rip accepted that there is no appeal from an assessment that no tax is payable (a "nil assessment"). None of the statutory remedies enumerated in subsection 171(1) could cure the appellant's grievance, as the amount assessed would remain nil regardless of the Court's findings on the underlying credit.

While Chief Justice Rip expressed pointed judicial sympathy—remarking that "it is simply not right for the Crown to act behind a nil assessment" to prevent Mr. Tozzi from applying for a disability savings plan—the Court concluded that it had no lawful jurisdiction to order the Minister to recognize the appellant's disability for RDSP purposes, no power to rule on his eligibility as an RDSP beneficiary without at the same time adjusting the amount of tax assessed, and no jurisdiction to review the administrative actions of CRA officials. Because section 146.4 of the Act, which regulates RDSPs, contains no provision similar to subsection 172(3)—which permits appeals to the Federal Court of Appeal from the Minister's refusal to register a Canadian amateur athletic association, a retirement savings plan, a profit sharing plan, an education savings plan and a pension plan—and because a review of the administrative actions of CRA officials is beyond the Tax Court's jurisdiction (Chief Justice Rip noting that the appellant may have redress in an application under section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, despite his agent's concern about the cost of Federal Court proceedings), the Court granted the respondent's motion and dismissed the appeal.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The inclusion of Giovanni Tozzi v. The Queen alongside cases such as Ben Martens v. M.N.R. (1988) and D. Nagel v. The Queen (2018) in specialized Canadian SR&ED case law indices reflects a critical operational reality of Canadian R&D tax practice. In the SR&ED regime, substantive technical disputes over technological uncertainty and systematic investigation are inextricably linked to the procedural posture of the taxpayer's corporate tax return (T2) or individual return (T1). When a claimant fails to synchronize their technical evidentiary defence with the statutory assessing mechanisms of section 152 of the Act, the CRA's denial of SR&ED expenditures and ITCs culminates in an unappealable nil assessment.
The Jurisdictional Mechanics of the Nil Assessment Bar in SR&ED Disputes

To comprehend how Tozzi governs SR&ED controversies, tax counsel must distinguish between the two statutory pillars of the Canadian SR&ED incentive program: first, the deduction of current and capital SR&ED expenditures via the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool; and second, the generation of Investment Tax Credits under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act.

For a qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) that meets the taxable income and taxable capital thresholds, SR&ED ITCs are earned at an enhanced rate of 35% on up to the expenditure limit and are partially or fully refundable under section 127.1 of the Act. Crucially, under paragraph 152(1)(b) of the Act, a refundable ITC is deemed to be a payment on account of Part I tax payable. When the Minister assesses a return and determines the amount of a deemed payment on account of tax under paragraph 152(1)(b)—even if the refund is denied in full following an audit—that determination gives rise to an objection and appeal right if properly triggered on the assessment or via a valid reassessment.

However, a vast segment of Canadian R&D claimants do not receive a refundable ITC determination under paragraph 152(1)(b). This includes public corporations that are not eligible Canadian public corporations, foreign-controlled corporations, partnerships, and CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds the statutory phase-out thresholds, all of which earn non-refundable ITCs at the basic 15% rate that can only be applied against Part I tax otherwise payable or carried back three years and forward twenty years. Furthermore, even a CCPC that files a Taxpayer Requested Adjustment (TPR) or utilizes permissive deductions—such as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) under paragraph 20(1)(a) or subsection 37(1) pool deductions—to bring taxable income to zero without a refundable credit balance receives a nil assessment.

When the CRA audits such a claimant, the RTA and FR compile a Financial Review Report (FRR) and issue a Form T7W-C explaining adjustments to Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations). If the CRA disallows the SR&ED claim in its entirety in a year where the corporation has no Part I tax payable, the resulting Notice of Assessment or Reassessment shows $0 tax owing. As applied in Tozzi and reaffirmed in subsequent jurisprudence up to Onischuk v. The King (2025 TCC 17), a nil assessment does not fix the underlying components of a taxpayer's income, tax pools, or non-refundable credits, and therefore cannot be objected to under section 165 or appealed to the Tax Court under section 169.
Failure to Trigger a Subsection 152(1.1) Notice of Determination of Loss

The primary procedural failure that traps SR&ED claimants in the Tozzi predicament is the failure to convert an unappealable nil assessment into a binding, appealable Notice of Determination/Redetermination of a Loss (Form T67AM) under subsection 152(1.1) of the Act.

Because the subsection 37(1) SR&ED expenditure pool is a permissive deduction—meaning a taxpayer may elect to deduct all, part, or none of the pool in a given taxation year and carry the undeducted balance forward indefinitely—many corporations in a loss position leave their claimed SR&ED expenditures sitting in the subsection 37(1) pool rather than deducting them to increase their non-capital loss for the year. Similarly, when the CRA denies an SR&ED claim, it reduces the ending balance of the subsection 37(1) pool and the non-refundable ITC pool on Schedule T2SCH31.

Under subsection 152(1.1), the Minister is only required to issue a formal Notice of Determination of Loss (NODL) when three strict statutory conditions are met: first, the Minister ascertains the amount of a taxpayer's non-capital, net capital, restricted farm, farm, or limited partnership loss for a taxation year; second, the taxpayer has requested the determination; and third, the loss amount ascertained by the Minister differs from the loss amount reported by the taxpayer in their return of income. If a taxpayer leaves its SR&ED expenditures in the subsection 37(1) pool (or only claims non-refundable ITCs without deducting the expenditures into its current-year non-capital loss), the CRA's disallowance of the SR&ED claim alters the subsection 37(1) pool and ITC schedule, but does not alter the taxpayer's reported non-capital loss for the year. Consequently, the statutory prerequisite for a subsection 152(1.1) loss determination is not met, no Form T67AM can be issued, and under Tozzi, the taxpayer is completely locked out of the Tax Court of Canada until a future profitable year when the credit or pool is actually applied against positive tax payable. As legal scholarship and cases such as Joshi v. The Queen and D. Nagel v. The Queen demonstrate, waiting years to litigate an SR&ED claim in a future profitable year is often fatal to the technical defence due to fading witness memory, employee turnover, and the degradation of technical evidence.
Substantive Technical & Evidentiary Failures Triggering Audit Disallowance

While the Tozzi doctrine governs the jurisdictional gateway to the Tax Court, a taxpayer only confronts a nil assessment after the CRA has denied the claim on substantive technical, financial, or statutory compliance grounds. In Canadian SR&ED practice, CRA audit denials recorded in the RTA report and FRR fall into four recurring evidentiary and legal categories.
Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty

Under subsection 248(1) of the Act, eligible SR&ED requires work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or technological advancement. In Canadian jurisprudence, technological advancement cannot exist without an underlying technological uncertainty—a fundamental limitation in the existing baseline of scientific or engineering knowledge that cannot be resolved through standard practice, publicly available techniques, or routine engineering. Taxpayers routinely fail this requirement by conflating commercial, functional, or project-level uncertainty ("will the product meet customer specifications on budget?") with true technological uncertainty ("can a specific system constraint or material incompatibility be overcome when existing engineering principles predict failure?"). When project narratives on Form T661 describe system integration, parameter optimization, or standard debugging, the RTA classifies the project under the statutory finding that "no work meets the definition of SR&ED".
Lack of a Structured Process of Experimentation (Systematic Investigation)

Even where a genuine technological obstacle exists, subsection 248(1) mandates a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The Tax Court requires proof of the scientific method applied to industrial R&D, encompassing the observation of the baseline technological limitation, the formulation of a specific and testable hypothesis designed to resolve the uncertainty, the execution of structured testing or analytical modelling, and the logical evaluation of quantifiable results leading to a technological conclusion or subsequent iterative hypothesis. Claimants frequently fail because their engineering teams engage in ad-hoc trial and error or undocumented troubleshooting, leaving the RTA to conclude that the work lacked systematic rigour.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and Prescribed Filing Failures

The CRA's FRR framework explicitly distinguishes between claims where "no work meets the definition of SR&ED" and claims where "work is unsubstantiated". Canadian courts consistently hold that oral testimony reconstructed years after the taxation year cannot substitute for contemporaneous documentation generated as the R&D progressed, such as dated test logs, failed prototype telemetry, source code commit histories showing experimental branches, and time-tracking records linking specific personnel to eligible activities.

Moreover, procedural documentation failures under subsection 37(11) of the Act are strictly fatal. Subsection 37(11) stipulates that no amount in respect of an SR&ED expenditure may be deducted under subsection 37(1) (or included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes) unless the taxpayer files with the Minister a prescribed form (Form T661) containing prescribed information (including the technical project descriptions and Schedule T2SCH31) on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year. As Justice Bowie held in 1373744 Ontario Inc. o/a One Source Metal v. Her Majesty The Queen (2009 TCC 511)—the companion compliance decision immediately preceding Tozzi in Canadian SR&ED case law indices—where the taxpayer's accountant stapled the 2005 and 2006 T661 packages (each with Schedules 31 and 1) and a separate technical report, paper-clipped the three documents together, and had them delivered to the Toronto West Tax Services Office on March 28, 2007—days before the March 31, 2007 deadline for the 2005 claim—but a CRA "received" stamp was obtained only on the file copies of the two T661 forms and not on the file copy of the technical report, the Court concluded on a balance of probabilities that the technical report was not filed until after the deadline, held that the appellant had not met its onus, and dismissed the appeal from the 2005 reassessment denying the SR&ED deduction.
Contractual and Funded Research Exclusions

Under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Act, qualified SR&ED expenditures must be reduced by any "government assistance," "non-government assistance," or "contract payment" that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive. A "contract payment" arises where a taxpayer performs R&D for or on behalf of another taxable Canadian supplier or customer pursuant to a commercial agreement. When a taxpayer drafts commercial supply or custom engineering agreements poorly—failing to separate standard commercial deliverables from independent, self-funded R&D, or transferring intellectual property and technical risk to the customer—the CRA recharacterizes the customer's revenue payments as "contract payments" in Section E.2 of the FRR. This recharacterization grinds the taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures down to zero, wipes out any refundable ITC deemed tax payment under paragraph 152(1)(b), and leaves the taxpayer with a nil assessment that—under Tozzi—cannot be appealed to the Tax Court.

The following table maps each statutory, jurisdictional, and technical requirement governing Canadian tax credit litigation and SR&ED claims against the specific taxpayer vulnerabilities exposed by Tozzi and related TCC jurisprudence, alongside the mandatory standard of proof required by the Court.

cells: Jurisdictional Threshold for Tax Court Appeals
Income Tax Act, ss. 169(1), 171(1); Tax Court of Canada Act, s. 12
Appealing a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment where $0 in Part I tax, interest, or penalty is assessed ("nil assessment") following the CRA's denial of a tax credit.

Absolute Jurisdictional Bar: The TCC can only vacate, vary, or refer back an assessment of tax payable (Tozzi, 2010 TCC 545; Okalta Oils; Interior Savings). An appeal from a nil assessment is dismissed on the respondent's preliminary motion.
Loss Determination & Pool Dispute Conversion
Income Tax Act, ss. 152(1.1), 152(1.2), 37(1), 111(1)(a)

Leaving disallowed SR&ED expenditures in the permissive s. 37(1) pool rather than deducting them into the current-year non-capital loss, or refusing to request a formal Notice of Determination of Loss (Onischuk, 2025 TCC 17).

Statutory Discrepancy Mandate: To obtain an appealable Form T67AM (NODL), the taxpayer must prove that the Minister ascertained a non-capital loss that differs from the loss reported on the taxpayer's return.
Refundable ITC Deemed Tax Payment Trigger
Income Tax Act, ss. 127(5), 127(9), 127.1, 152(1)(b)

Losing CCPC refundable ITC eligibility (or filing an unassessed post-return TPR where credits are non-refundable), thereby failing to trigger a paragraph 152(1)(b) determination of a deemed payment on account of tax.
Deemed Payment Verification: Under s. 152(1)(b), an appeal lies only if the Minister formally assesses or determines the quantum of a refundable credit deemed paid on account of Part I tax.
Review of CRA Administrative Conduct
Federal Courts Act, s. 18.1; Income Tax Act, s. 172(3)
Petitioning the Tax Court of Canada to issue a declaratory order recognizing credit eligibility or reviewing unfair administrative conduct by CRA officials behind a nil assessment.

Forum Exclusivity: The TCC has no jurisdiction to review the administrative actions of CRA officials; per Tozzi, such review is beyond the Court's jurisdiction. Tozzi indicates the taxpayer may have redress by an application in the Federal Court under s. 18.1, which must generally be brought within 30 days under s. 18.1(2).
Prescribed Form & 12-Month Filing Deadline
Income Tax Act, s. 37(11); Form T661; Schedule T2SCH31

Failing to file Form T661 and complete technical descriptions within 12 months of the tax return filing due date, or failing to retain date-stamped proof of receipt for every component (One Source Metal, 2009 TCC 511).

Strict Statutory Compliance: Balance of probabilities requiring objective, verifiable proof (CRA electronic transmission confirmation or official date stamp on every separate document) that prescribed information was received before the 12-month bar.
Technological Uncertainty & Advancement
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1) ("SR&ED"); Income Tax Regulations, s. 2900
Describing commercial goals, functional product features, or routine engineering / system integration on Form T661 without isolating fundamental system-level or scientific limitations.

Objective Technical Standard: Demonstrating via expert-grade technical evidence that the objective could not be achieved using publicly available knowledge or standard engineering practice, and that the work generated new technological knowledge.
Systematic Investigation & Contemporaneous Evidence
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1), 230(1); CRA FRR Audit Standards
Relying on trial-and-error development and retroactive oral testimony rather than hypothesis-driven testing logs generated during the taxation year ("work is unsubstantiated").

Contemporaneous Documentary Proof: Establishing a structured sequence of hypothesis formulation, iterative experimental testing, and quantitative analysis supported by dated contemporaneous artifacts created during the claim year.
Contractual & Funded Research Exclusions
Income Tax Act, ss. 37(1)(d), 127(9) ("contract payment", "assistance")
Executing commercial supply contracts where the customer funds development or acquires IP rights, allowing CRA to grind qualified SR&ED expenditures to nil as a "contract payment".

Substance Over Form Contractual Analysis: Proving through written contract terms, IP ownership clauses, and financial risk allocation that R&D was performed on the taxpayer's own account and not "for or on behalf of" the customer.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings of Giovanni Tozzi v. The Queen and the statutory architecture of sections 37, 127, and 152 of the Income Tax Act into actionable legal and technical practice, the following two industry case studies examine realistic Canadian corporate claimants confronting the exact intersection of technical audit disallowances and the nil assessment jurisdictional bar.
Case Study 1: Advanced Metallurgical & Automated Stamping Systems (Ontario Non-Refundable ITC Claimant in a Loss Position)
Industry Scenario and Impending Legal Pitfalls

A Mississauga, Ontario-based industrial manufacturer ("MetalloTech Inc.") designs high-tonnage progressive die-stamping systems for ultra-high-strength steel (UHSS) automotive chassis components. Because MetalloTech Inc. was recently acquired by a foreign publicly traded parent corporation (or exceeded the taxable capital phase-out threshold for CCPCs), it is no longer eligible for the 35% enhanced refundable ITC under section 127.1; instead, it earns non-refundable 15% ITCs under subsection 127(5).

In its fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, MetalloTech incurred $1.8 million in SR&ED expenditures attempting to eliminate hydrogen-induced micro-cracking and unpredictable springback during high-velocity cold stamping of 1,500 MPa martensitic steel. Due to heavy capital investments and market headwinds, MetalloTech reported a net operating loss for 2025. To preserve its subsection 37(1) SR&ED expenditure pool for future profitable years, MetalloTech's external accountants elected not to deduct the $1.8 million from the subsection 37(1) pool on Schedule 1, leaving its reported non-capital loss unaffected by the SR&ED claim, and filed paper schedules near the 12-month subsection 37(11) deadline without unified electronic confirmation.

Upon audit, the CRA RTA concluded that MetalloTech's work was routine die-tooling calibration ("no work meets the definition of SR&ED") and the FR issued an FRR disallowing the entire $1.8 million subsection 37(1) pool addition and $270,000 in non-refundable ITCs. Because MetalloTech owed $0 in Part I tax both before and after the audit, the Minister issued a nil assessment for 2025. Under Tozzi, any Notice of Objection or Tax Court appeal filed by MetalloTech against the 2025 assessment will be dismissed on a preliminary Crown motion, as Mr. Tozzi's appeal was, and because the disallowance only reduced the undeducted subsection 37(1) pool without altering the reported non-capital loss, the Minister refuses to issue a subsection 152(1.1) Notice of Determination of Loss.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Procedural & Tax Return Governance to Defeat the Tozzi Nil Assessment Bar

To prevent the CRA from insulating its technical audit denial behind an unappealable nil assessment, MetalloTech must restructure how it reports permissive deductions on its T2 Corporate Income Tax Return. Rather than leaving the $1.8 million of SR&ED expenditures parked in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool during a loss year, tax counsel must instruct the corporate tax preparer to deduct the full $1.8 million from the subsection 37(1) pool on Schedule 1 in the year incurred, thereby directly increasing the corporation's reported non-capital loss for the taxation year.

Because non-capital losses can be carried forward 20 years under section 111, converting the subsection 37(1) pool into a current-year non-capital loss preserves the deduction while fundamentally altering the procedural litigation posture. When the CRA RTA and FR disallow the $1.8 million SR&ED claim, the disallowance directly reduces the corporation's reported non-capital loss by $1.8 million. This creates the exact statutory discrepancy required by subsection 152(1.1): the loss ascertained by the Minister now differs from the loss reported by the taxpayer. Immediately upon receipt of the nil reassessment, MetalloTech serves a formal demand under subsection 152(1.1) requiring the Minister to issue Form T67AM (Notice of Determination/Redetermination of a Loss). Once Form T67AM is issued, subsection 152(1.2) makes the objection and appeal provisions of sections 165 and 169 fully applicable, completely bypassing the Tozzi nil assessment bar and granting MetalloTech an immediate right to a de novo trial in the Tax Court of Canada.
Step 2: Technical Governance & Reframing Technological Uncertainty

To overturn the RTA's characterization of the stamping trials as "routine die calibration," MetalloTech must restructure its project governance around fundamental materials science and metallurgical uncertainty. Prior to commencing physical trials, the engineering team must author a formal Baseline Technological Limitation Charter establishing that standard Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulation software and published metallurgical forming limit diagrams (FLDs) fail to predict non-linear adiabatic shear banding and delayed hydrogen embrittlement when stamping 1,500 MPa martensitic steels at stroke rates exceeding 45 strokes per minute. By framing the objective not as "producing an automotive bracket within dimensional tolerance," but as "developing a predictive thermo-mechanical model correlating localized die-radius friction coefficients and rapid strain-rate work-hardening to suppress lattice micro-void nucleation," MetalloTech anchors the claim squarely within subsection 248(1) technological advancement.
Step 3: Systematic Experimentation Tracking

MetalloTech must replace ad-hoc press adjustments with a structured Design of Experiments (DoE) ledger in which each experimental iteration is logged as a discrete hypothesis-test-analysis cycle. At the outset of each test series, the engineering team must explicitly formulate the causal metallurgical hypothesis being evaluated, such as postulating that dynamically varying the nitrogen-cushioned blank-holder pressure profile during the initial 15 milliseconds of draw depth will reduce peak tensile residual stress below the 650 MPa hydrogen diffusion threshold. During controlled execution and quantitative analysis, engineers must record high-frequency press telemetry alongside destructive metallographic cross-sectioning and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) crack-density measurements. Finally, the team must document a logical analytical conclusion explaining why the hypothesis succeeded or failed, thereby proving the generation of new engineering knowledge regardless of whether the physical stamped part was scrapped.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Documentation & Subsection 37(11) Filing Controls

To eliminate the One Source Metal (2009 TCC 511) filing vulnerability, MetalloTech must prohibit paper-clipped or manually delivered physical T661 submissions. All T661 forms, Part 2 technical project descriptions, and Schedule T2SCH31 schedules must be transmitted electronically via the CRA's Corporation Internet Filing system at least 60 days prior to the 12-month subsection 37(11) statutory deadline, generating an immutable, system-stamped confirmation number that covers both the financial schedules and the embedded technical narrative. Concurrently, all labour hours claimed on Form T661 must be reconciled monthly to activity-coded engineering timesheets cross-referenced to specific DoE experiment numbers.

Technological Uncertainty Framing

Isolating non-linear adiabatic shear banding and hydrogen diffusion thresholds in 1,500 MPa martensitic steel.
Experimentation Methodology

Formal Design of Experiments (DoE) correlating FEA simulations, dynamic blank-holder pressure hypotheses, and SEM crack-density telemetry.
Prescribed Form Filing Compliance

Unified electronic T2/T661/T2SCH31 transmission 60 days prior to the s. 37(11) deadline with activity-coded timesheet reconciliation.

body.text: Case Study 2: Distributed AI & Edge-Computing Telemetry Architecture (Quebec CCPC Facing Contract Payment Disallowance and Nil Assessment)
Industry Scenario and Impending Legal Pitfalls

A Montreal, Quebec-based software engineering firm ("NeuroEdge Technologies Inc."), structured as a CCPC, develops low-latency neural network quantization algorithms for industrial robotics. In its 2025 taxation year, NeuroEdge entered into a $1.2 million commercial agreement with a major Canadian aerospace prime contractor ("AeroPrime Corp.") to deliver an embedded real-time anomaly-detection software module. NeuroEdge incurred $950,000 in Quebec and federal SR&ED salary expenditures on the project and claimed a 35% enhanced refundable federal ITC under sections 127(5) and 127.1. Because NeuroEdge reinvested all revenues into growth and utilized prior-year non-capital losses and discretionary deductions to reduce its taxable income to zero, it owed $0 in Part I tax.

During a joint technical and financial review, the CRA FR examined the commercial master services agreement between NeuroEdge and AeroPrime. Because the contract stated that NeuroEdge would "design, develop, test, and deliver the anomaly-detection software to AeroPrime's specifications" and granted AeroPrime ownership of all custom software deliverables upon payment of milestone invoices, the CRA classified the entire $1.2 million commercial revenue as a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9). In Sections E.2 and E.3 of the FRR, the CRA reduced NeuroEdge's qualified SR&ED expenditures from $950,000 to $0, eliminated the refundable ITC in full, and—because the claim had been submitted via an unassessed post-return Taxpayer Requested Adjustment (TPR) or offset against non-taxable balances—issued a nil assessment notification for 2025. Furthermore, the RTA asserted that NeuroEdge's software development constituted routine adaptation of open-source deep learning libraries. Under Tozzi, when NeuroEdge attempts to appeal the 2025 nil assessment to the Tax Court of Canada to argue the contractual and technical issues, the Crown moves to dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring to Eliminate the "Contract Payment" Grind

To prevent customer payments from extinguishing qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(9), NeuroEdge's legal counsel must redraft its commercial agreements prior to execution to sever the nexus between the commercial deliverable and the underlying SR&ED. The agreement must be structured strictly as a commercial product supply or software licensing contract for a finished functional output, explicitly excluding any covenant or obligation requiring NeuroEdge to perform scientific research or experimental development "for or on behalf of" AeroPrime. Furthermore, the contract must incorporate an explicit intellectual property retention clause stipulating that all background and foreground intellectual property, core quantization algorithms, neural network weights, and architectural methodologies developed by NeuroEdge remain the sole and exclusive property of NeuroEdge, while AeroPrime receives only a non-exclusive licence to operate the compiled binary object code within its aerospace hardware.
